Field surveys at Anse du Halage have provided extensive data on the life history of the Kerguelen sea urchin Abatus cordatus. Among the most notable findings is the maximum observed length recorded for individuals at this station, which reaches 4.2 cm . The ultimate maximum length, representing the theoretical upper bound of somatic growth, is considerably larger at 8 cm [Li = 8 cm], a value that highlights the substantial growth potential this species retains even in the cold, food-limited waters of the sub-Antarctic. In reproductively active females sampled at Anse du Halage after roughly ten months of gonad maturation, the gonadosomatic index (GSI) reached 7% [GSI = 7%] at an ambient water temperature of 5 °C [T = 5 °C].

The early developmental stages of Abatus cordatus at Anse du Halage are characterized by specific morphological and mass benchmarks. The length at metamorphosis, marking the transition from a planktonic larva to a benthic juvenile, is 0.276 cm . Concurrently, the wet weight at metamorphosis for these newly settled individuals is measured at 0.0103 grams . Prior to this transformation, the initial investment in offspring is reflected in the wet weight of the egg, which is 0.001777 grams [Ww0 = 0.001777 grams]. These small but energetically rich eggs are brooded by the female, a reproductive mode that is relatively uncommon among echinoids but well-documented in the genus Abatus. The progression from these minute eggs to a juvenile mass that is nearly an order of magnitude larger indicates a reliance on maternal provisioning during the encapsulated phase, which occurs at the consistently cold temperatures of the region.

Reproductive maturity in this brooding echinoid is attained at a well-defined size and mass. At Anse du Halage, the length at puberty is recorded as 1.9 cm [Lp = 1.9 cm], and the corresponding wet weight at puberty is 2.9 grams [Wwp = 2.9 grams]. These values mark the point at which individuals begin to invest in gonadal development and, for females, the commencement of brooding behavior. The time required to reach this developmental milestone was studied under controlled laboratory conditions that mimicked the local thermal regime. At a stable temperature of 5 °C [T = 5 °C], the first successful spawning event was found to occur approximately 1098 days after metamorphosis [tR = approximately 1098 days after metamorphosis]. This exceptionally long pre-reproductive period, spanning nearly three years, is a hallmark of a slow life history and is closely tied to the low metabolic rates imposed by the persistently cold polar waters of the Kerguelen Plateau.

The complete life cycle of Abatus cordatus unfolds over a duration that is substantial for an echinoid of its size. The maximum lifespan recorded for individuals maintained under conditions mimicking their natural habitat, specifically at a temperature of 5 °C [T = 5 °C], is approximately 2190 days [am = approximately 2190 days]. This longevity is complemented by data on the maximum observed wet weight, which for adults at Anse du Halage reaches 25 grams . The time required for the critical metamorphic transition from larva to juvenile was also determined under these thermal conditions. Metamorphosis, which marks the end of the larval period, occurs after 142 days since hatching  at a temperature of 5 °C [T = 5 °C]. The combination of a long larval phase, a delayed onset of reproduction, and a multi-year adult lifespan forms a coherent life-history package that is well-adapted to the stable but resource-poor environment of the Southern Ocean.

The ecological context of Anse du Halage provides a valuable framework for interpreting these life-history parameters. The populations of Abatus cordatus inhabiting this site experience a pronounced seasonal cycle in primary productivity, which directly influences food availability for this deposit-feeding species. Growth to the maximum structural length of 8 cm [Li = 8 cm] would require an extended period of favorable conditions, which are not always guaranteed in this environment; the observed maximum length of 4.2 cm  therefore likely represents the actual size attained by most individuals given local energetic constraints. Similarly, the wet weight at puberty of 2.9 grams [Wwp = 2.9 grams] and the corresponding length at puberty of 1.9 cm [Lp = 1.9 cm] serve as critical thresholds that individuals must cross before they begin to invest energy in reproduction. In ripe females at station Anse du Halage, the GSI was 7% [GSI = 7%] after about ten months of gonad maturation, measured at 5 °C [T = 5 °C].
